sentences.text: Senior Standing Counsel  ORDER (Order of the Court was made by J.NISHA BANU, J.)

Challenging the Regulation 2.3.12 of the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restriction on Sale) Regulations, 2011 dated 25.06.2019,
which prohibits sale of the common salt for direct human consumption as well as Regulation 2.4.42 of the Food Safety Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011, this writ petition is filed seeking to declare those Regulations as null and void and ultra vires of the Constitution of India with a consequential direction to the respondents 1 to 3 to permit the petitioner to have the following label bearing words 'Non-Iodised Common Salt' on the package of Common Salt and on the package of Iodised Salt as 'Iodised salt-A Necessary Nutrient'.

2. The facts leading to the filing of the writ petition are as follows:
2.1.
Originally, the petitioner-salt association filed this writ petition to quash the Regulation 2.3.12 dated 31.07.2018 banning the common salt for human consumption as null and void.
Later, by an amendment dated 25.06.2019, the prohibition was mandated for direct human consumption and consumption related activities.
The respondents' counter affidavits dealt with labelling procedures also.
Therefore, the petitioner has amended the prayer.
2.2. According to the petitioner, this is the third round of wrongful amendment arbitrarily done by the respondents.
In the first round of litigation, when the ban on sale of common salt was introduced through Rule 44-I of PFA Rules in the year 2005, the challenge to it went upto the Supreme Court.

In the judgment reported in (2011) 8 SCC 274, the Apex Court ruled that rule 44-I of the Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules 1955, was beyond the rule making power of the Central Government and ultra vires of the PFA Act.

The Apex Court granted six months time to review the compulsory iodization policy and https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on:
19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) come out with an appropriate legislation or other measures, if such policy should continue in future.

In the second round of litigation in the year 2012, the Government again brought into force the said ban through the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act,
2006.

Granting the interim stay until disposal of W.Ps., the first bench of the Madras High Court, by a common order dated 13.4.2006 passed in W.P.Nos. 22470 of 2012 etc., batch filed by various salt traders, held that on account of constituting a Committee to undertake a comprehensive review of the said Act, the writ petitions were disposed of to examine all the issues and to put forth the objections raised by various associations to be considered in spirit and substance, failing which, the Division Bench granted liberty to revive even the earlier W.Ps, though such a chance may not arise on account of formation of a Committee to review.

The fact remains that the Tuticorin Salt Association, being the second biggest association in the Country next to Gujarat, was neither consulted nor called for revisiting the matter with technical and scientific data and so on.

3. The learned counsel appearing for the petitioner would submit that the respondents have brought the above amendment on the sole ground that there shall be an iodine intake of 150mg in adults daily who are not pregnant or lactating.
lodine is said to be a micronutrient that is essential for the production of thyroid hormones.
The primary source of iodine is the diet via consumption of foods fortified with iodine, including salt.
Therefore, the respondents thought that the only way to infuse 150mg of iodine into the human body is by way of using the iodized salt.

Consequently, it was unanimously decided by the respondents that if the sale of common salt for human consumption and its allied activities are banned, the public would be constrained to use only the iodized salt and hence the purpose could be achieved.

This is the sum and substance of the entire amendment behind banning the sale of common salt in terms of the existing Food Safety and Standards Act,
2006.
4.

The learned counsel would further contend that with a view to enrich certain lobbying manufacturers of iodized salt, impugned amendment has been brought into force as if the entire country is suffering from lodine Deficiency Disorder (IDD) and therefore, the https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) whole Country
should follow the pattern of lodized salt in human consumption.
If that is done, it will cause Goiter and related ailments.
The learned counsel would further state that if a food item is to be banned, it should either be an adulterated one or injurious to health.
Admittedly, the manufacture of common salt is not injurious to health and there is no adulteration in it.
On the other hand, it is a natural and wholesome food item made with three natural ingredients namely, water, sunlight and air.
The process of manufacture is also on the open field with exposure to sunlight from one segment of storage to another segment of storage, by which temperature is increased for making common salt.
At the optimum level, the common salt gets formed and it is used for human consumption.
Apart from using the common salt for cooking purpose, for over thousand years, it has been used as a medicinal purpose.
It is an admitted fact that iodine deficiency disorder (IDD) is not pandemic in any Country and it may be endemic in some parts of the country.
Therefore, the impugned amendment banning sale of common salt, is opposed to the very object of the Act and the rule making power of the Central Government.
Consequently, the above Regulation 2.3.12 requires to be declared as null and void and ultra vires of the Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India.

The scientists and research institutes have opined that excess iodine is life threatening and it results in throat cancer and hyperthyroidism.
However, taking a stand that if there is no proper iodine intake, it will result in Goiter in the throat region, the iodized salt lobby is attempting to enter into the commercial market.

The Panel further stated that an average individual consumes 10 grams https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) of salt per day in India.

6. It is further submitted that FSSAI stated that a new standard for low sodium salt is currently under consideration of Authority.
Besides, the irony is that the iodized salt is also made out of common salt only, by way of eliminating minerals such as Calcium, Magnesium, Zinc and so on.
The iodized salt is bleached with chemical to make it artificially whiter than that of natural common salt and it causes a lot of medical issues to regular users.
Therefore, the petitioner contends that there cannot be any legislation on the choice of using a food item.
As of today, there are several research articles and publications touching upon the medical consequences of using iodized salt.
Ultimately it has come to the stage of low value iodine salt.
On the other hand, the respondents say that iodized salt shall not be used for human consumption by pregnant women and lactating mothers.

Therefore,
if the sale of common salt is banned, those segments of women cannot have any alternative.

Moreover, the slightly extended form of common salt known as "rock salt", "Himalayan pink salt".
etc., also contain the same ingredients as that of common salt.

Through the online sale, common https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) salt is sold to the public at large and they are not prohibited or banned for the sale of human consumption.
As enclosed in pages 47 to 50 of the main typed set, in USA and Australia also, common salt is sold to the public as an edible item.

Thus, it will meet the ends of justice and at the same time comply with requirements of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 if the petitioner and similar salt traders are allowed to sell the common salt for human consumption by labelling them in a proper way, so that any member of the public will know what type of salt he or she is buying.
Hence, the learned counsel would pray for setting aside the impugned Regulations and to issue consequential direction as sought for.

sentences.text: The Iodine content of commonly used plant food is very low and far below the Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA).
Further, the amount of thiocyanate, a goitrogen, is high in plant foods which affect the iodine utilization in the human system.
Therefore, iodine supplementation to the entire population is essential.

Surveys conducted by several agencies including Directorate General of Health Services, ICMR, State Govts. & Health Institutions have revealed that no State/UT in India is free from Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD).

Out of 427 districts surveyed (up to 2017-18) in all the https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on:
19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) 29 States and 7 Union Territories so far, 348 districts are endemic i.e where the prevalence of Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDDs) is more than 5%.

Due to soil erosion,
there is a deficiency of iodine in foods including cereals, pulses, fruits, vegetables etc grown on such soil.

The famous Kangra valley study conducted by AllMS, New Delhi, from 1956 to 1972 proved beyond doubt that lodised salt given to defined population of the district brought down prevalence of Goitre from 40% to 5% within a few years.
The success of this study lead to launch of National Goitre Control Programme (NGCP) in 1962 by the Government of India.
Consumption of iodated salt is the cheapest method to control Iodine Deficiency Disorders in the country.
Salt is best medium for supply of iodine to the entire population since it is universally consumed by all the population.
WHO and UNICEF have also recommended universal salt iodization since 1993, as stated in WHO guidelines.

It reads as follows:
''No person shall sell or offer or expose for sale or have in premises for the purpose of sale, the common salt for direct human consumption unless the same is iodised.

Provided that common salt may be sold or exposed for sale or stored for sale for iodisation, iron fortification, animal sue, preservation, manufacturing medicine,
industrial use, under proper label declarations as specified under Clause 22 of sub-rule (zzz) of rule 42.''
11. It was further submitted that Rule 44-I of PFA Rules, was challenged before various High Courts and before the Hon'ble Supreme Court.
The petitions pending before various High Courts on the issue https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) were transferred to Supreme Court for proper adjudication.

The Apex Court vide its Judgment dated 04.07.2011 decided the matter and considered the following question of law:-

entities.text: Thuthukudi Thanpadu Uppu Ettrumathi ... vs Union Of India on 13 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon

sentences.text: As regards question No.(i), the Apex Court held that Rule 44-I is not unconstitutional and therefore rejected the contention that the provisions placing ban on sale of non-iodised communal salt for human consumption resulting in compulsory intake of iodised salt is not violative of Article 14 and 21 of the Constitution of India.
As regards question No.(ii), the Apex Court held that making available medicine or medicinal preparations to improve public health was not the object of the PFA Act.
The object of the Act was to eliminate the danger to human life from the sale of adulterated food and to ensure wholesome food to general public.
The Court had further held that the Act cannot be used to make a rule intended to achieve an object wholly unrelated to the Act.
Therefore, Rule 44-I was wholly outside the scope of the Act.

sentences.text: The 1st respondent through NIDDCP continuously tracks the implementation of Sale iodization and evaluates it's health benefits by gathering data from all states periodically.

The Government of India has taken note of scientific and medical inputs, research results and survey data to conclude that compulsory iodisation is the most effective and accepted method for elimination of iodine deficiency disorders(IDD) and that consumption of iodised salt by persons not suffering from iodine deficiency will not adversely affect them.
The impugned regulation is implementation of a policy decision of the Government regarding public health.
The material placed by the petitioners is not sufficient to hold that the reason for the ban is erroneous and that is unreasonable and arbitrary.

15. As regards the contention of the petitioner that regular intake of iodised salt, is injurious to the health of general populace, learned Additional Solicitor General would submit that the said allegation is unfounded.
The use of common salt (non-iodised salt) for industrial and commercial purpose is not prohibited and the ban operates only in regard to use of common salt for human consumption.

The further contention of the petitioner that compulsory iodization https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) program is intended to help foreign companies is unsubstantiated and driven by malice.

The argument that Article 19(1)(g)
is violated, is also liable to be rejected as there is no ban on production and supply of common salt for industrial, fish curing, Tanning, agriculture and other various purposes.

16. Learned Additional Solicitor General would also submit that right to health is a essential component of right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India and the impugned Regulation 2.3.12 which addresses health concerns, such as those associated with iodine deficiency align with the spirit of Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
The report prepared in partnership with UNICEF highlights significant progress made in implementing NIDDCP and ensuring iodine nutrition for the populace.

It commends the Government of India's effective strategies particularly,
the mandatory legislation on iodized salt as a crucial factor in the successful control of IDD.
17.
Learned Additional Solicitor General would add that the issue whether there should be universal salt iodisation is a much debated technical issue relating to medical science.
An informed https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) decision in such matters
can only be taken by experts after carrying out exhaustive surveys, trials, tests, scientific investigations and research.
The Courts are neither equipped, nor can be expected to decide about the need or absence of need for such universal salt iodisation on the basis of some articles and reports placed before it.
The Hon'ble Apex court as well this Hon'ble Court in a series of decisions has reiterated that Courts should not rush in where even scientists and medical experts are careful to tread.

The rule of prudence is that courts will be reluctant to interfere with policy decisions taken by the Government, in matters of public health, after collecting and analysing inputs from surveys and research.

Nor will courts attempt to substitute their own views as to what is wise, safe, prudent or proper, in relation to technical issues relating to public health in preference to those formulated by persons said to possess technical expertise and rich experience.

The petitioner's contention that India's salt policy should mirror that of developed countries, where consumers have a choice between iodized and non-iodized salt, overlooks the significant difference in population size, health awareness and economic conditions.
Further, the proposal to supplement the iodine through other foods like, fish and eggs is not viable due to their prohibitive cost and limited accessibility for average citizen.
Iodine deficiency is a pressing health concern that requires protective measures.

Given the well documented consequences of iodine deficiency, including goitre, physical and mental retardation and its impact of people of all ages and socio-economic, statuses, advocating flexible approach to iodized salt policy is untenable.
The petitioner's demand for further studies through AYUSH is unwarranted, in view of the availability of robust scientific data and established solution.

which prohibits sale of the common salt for direct human consumption as well as Regulation 2.4.42 of the Food Safety Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011, this writ petition is filed seeking to declare those Regulations as null and void and ultra vires of the Constitution of India with a consequential direction to the respondents 1 to 3 to permit the petitioner to have the following label bearing words 'Non-Iodised Common Salt' on the package of Common Salt and on the package of Iodised Salt as 'Iodised salt-A Necessary Nutrient'.
In the first round of litigation, when the ban on sale of common salt was introduced through Rule 44-I of PFA Rules in the year 2005, the challenge to it went upto the Supreme Court.
